_note: One line per testimony day: what that day shows about how a survivor's account is heard. Shown on each day page under 'Toward the march', linking to the finale. Written for Corey's voice; edit here, nothing else changes.

lines.line: Before any witness spoke, each side told the jury what the years meant. A survivor's account almost always arrives with a second story already beside it.
The testimony began with ages and years, not one night. Survivors are often asked to account for years at a time.
The grid asks what backs her word. Survivors are often asked for proof that most harm never leaves behind.
Her old messages were read back to her and asked to mean something. A survivor's own words are often turned into the case against her.
Ventura's fourth and last day on the stand. Telling your own life to a room of strangers is part of what speaking up can cost.
Other people said they saw violence, or what it left behind. Many survivors have no one who saw.
Money went to Combs and came back. Money can be one of the ways a person is held in place.
Most of the people on this chart waited years before telling anyone official. Waiting is common, and it is not the same as making it up.
Hotel records showed stays under other names. What stays hidden shapes who is believed later.
Seven accounts of one month. A survivor's account is rarely the only one, but it is often the only one questioned.
The investigation of the car fire stopped without a charge. Many survivors' reports end the same way: without an answer.
Workdays without an end, in Mia's account. Control over someone's time is one of the ways control works.
Money asked for, settled and received. Survivors who seek payment are often told that money is all they wanted.
Posts that praised him, beside what she said was happening. What a person shows in public and what she lives in private can both be true.
Cash for a hotel video, by the prosecution's account. Evidence of harm can be bought, kept or buried.
One video, followed from a hotel camera to the jury room. Most harm is never recorded at all.
A hotel bill tested a witness's date. Survivors are often tested hardest on when, not on what.
How long the nights lasted, in two women's testimony. This site counts hours so that it never has to describe them.
After the lawsuit, the people around Combs moved one by one. One person speaking up changes things for everyone near her.
Motions, rulings and immunity orders. The law decides which words a jury may hear, and from whom.
Every payment named in Jane's testimony. Survivors who were paid are often asked whether they were really harmed.
Six days on the stand, hour by hour. A survivor who testifies is questioned about her whole life, not one night.
Three searches, counted item by item. Things can be counted exactly while what they mean is still argued.
Twelve seats, and who sat in them changed. Who is on a jury shapes who is heard.
What the news said the jury was shown. Most survivors never see any of their evidence shown at all.
The staff around Combs, in their own testimony. Harm that lasts for years usually has help, knowing or not.
Trips across state lines: the only charges that ended in guilty verdicts. What can be proved is often narrower than what was lived.
The prosecution called 34 witnesses; the defense called none, as is its right. The burden of proof sat with the government, as it should. Outside a courtroom, survivors usually carry it alone.
